Last summer, my grandfather Chetan Dadu gave me a riddle: three friends, three pets, and five clues. Who owns the parrot?

I was eleven and I wanted to guess right away. Dadu said, "Don't guess. Draw it."

So I drew a grid, names down the side and pets across. Clue one said the girl doesn't own the dog, so I crossed that box. Clue two said the parrot owner lives next to the boy. That knocked out another.

I got confused on clue four and had to start over. But step by step, only one box was left. The parrot belonged to the girl.

I ran to Dadu. He just smiled and said, "Now you know how to think it through, Dhruv."

qa.q: What did Dhruv draw to solve the riddle?
qa.a: Dhruv drew a grid, with names down the side and pets across.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel when he got confused on clue four?
qa.a: Dhruv felt stuck and had to start over, but didn't give up.

qa.q: Why did Dadu's advice "Don't guess. Draw it" help?
qa.a: It made Dhruv work through each clue step by step, crossing out options until only one answer was left.

qa.q: How does Chetan Dadu seem to see Dhruv's effort?
qa.a: He seems pleased and quietly proud, glad that Dhruv learned to reason instead of guessing.

grounding: A child recalls solving a logic riddle step by step using a grid, working through confusion.

Jomon, nine, got stuck on today's number sequence: 2, 5, 11, 23, ?. He first said "30" and looked confused when it didn't fit. I asked him what happens between each pair. He wrote the gaps: 3, 6, 12. "They double!" he said. So the next gap is 24, and the answer is 47.

passage:
Tuesday night
Ganga Nani gave me a riddle at dinner. “A farmer has a goat, a tiger and a bundle of grass. His boat can carry him and one thing. If he leaves the goat with the grass, the goat eats it. If he leaves the tiger with the goat, the tiger eats the goat. How does he get them all across?”
I was confused for ages. Then I drew it on a napkin. First take the goat. Come back. Take the tiger. Bring the goat BACK. Take the grass. Come back for the goat.
Nani clapped. “Step by step, Zubin!”
I felt like a detective. — Zubin

qa.q: What can the farmer's boat carry?
qa.a: His boat can carry him and one thing.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel after solving the riddle?
qa.a: Zubin felt proud and clever, like a detective, after being confused for ages.

qa.q: What helped Zubin solve the riddle?
qa.a: Drawing it on a napkin and working through it step by step, including bringing the goat back.

qa.q: How did Ganga Nani feel when Zubin solved it?
qa.a: She felt delighted and proud, clapping for him.

grounding: A ten-year-old solves a logic riddle step by step by drawing it out.

In their village near Raipur, three new mango saplings had been chewed overnight. Sarita, nine, and her brother Shankar went to look.
“The Patils' goat,” said Shankar. “It always escapes.”
Sarita crouched. “Wait. Goat hooves are split. These prints are round, with toes.”
“A dog?”
“Dogs don't eat leaves.” She followed the prints to the fence. A gap at the bottom, small. And a bit of grey fur.
“A rabbit!” said Shankar.
“So the goat's not guilty,” Sarita said. “And the gap is how it gets in.”
They blocked it with stones.

qa.a: A small gap at the bottom and a bit of grey fur.

qa.a: She felt focused and curious, eager to work out the real culprit.

qa.a: She looked at the evidence step by step, ruling out the goat and the dog before finding the rabbit's way in.

qa.a: He is probably impressed, since she found a clue he missed.

I'm Alka, and I sat next to Rukmini during the riddle hunt at the community centre.
The clue said: "I am behind the thing that holds water, but not in the kitchen."
Rukmini tapped her pencil on her chin. "Holds water: tap, bucket, pot, tank." She crossed out "tap" and "pot". "Those are in the kitchen."
"Bucket's in the bathroom," I said.
"Tank's on the roof." She looked at the ladder. "But the roof's locked. So… bathroom."
She ran off. She came back waving the next clue from behind the bucket. I couldn't tell if she was proud or just happy, but she was grinning.

Irawati, you're stuck on that riddle? Come, I'll tell you how I learned to solve these, when I was ten.
I, Vikas, a skinny boy of ten, loved riddles but hated maths. My uncle gave me this one: a man has three sons, each son has one sister. How many children?
I shouted "six!" He laughed. "Slow down. Draw it."
I drew three boys. Then one sister for each. Then I saw: the same sister. Four children.
After that I drew every puzzle. Step by step, no shouting answers. My maths got better too.
So, Irawati, get a pencil. Draw it.

qa.a: The uncle likely felt pleased and proud of his nephew.

"Yogesh, puzzle time!" Sumit waved a paper. It was Diwali vacation, and the boys were bored.
"Three boxes of sweets. One has only ladoos, one only barfis, one mixed. All the labels are wrong. You can pick one sweet from one box. Which box?"
Yogesh frowned. "Any box?"
"Think."
"If I pick from 'Ladoos'… it's wrong, so it could be barfis or mixed. That doesn't help." He chewed his pencil. "But 'Mixed' is wrong for sure. So it's all ladoos or all barfis!"
"And?"
"If I pull a ladoo, that box is ladoos. Then 'Barfis' can't be barfis or ladoos, so it's mixed!"
Sumit groaned. "You got it faster than me."

qa.a: There were three boxes of sweets.

qa.a: He felt excited and confident, because he saw that the wrong label told him something for sure.

qa.q: What could Yogesh try on the next puzzle?
